gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much energy the 2 kWh candidates actually delivered in named tests. Notebookcheck got about 1,900 Wh at a ~250 W load from the $899.99 Anker SOLIX S2000. It got only about 1,600 Wh at ~200 W from the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2. StorageReview measured 1,800 Wh from the EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max and 1.91 kWh from the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2. OutdoorGearLab measured 1,710 Wh from the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2.
standout_why: theoutagebrief.com (cited) and generatorandbackup.com (cited) both say they did not test any unit and give only maker specs. powersized.com/solar-generator-kits (cited) has only OutdoorGearLab's panel-output range of 56–91% of rated watts and Jackery's own charge-time estimates. powersized.com/best/solar-generator (cited) is the only rival with a measured usable-capacity figure, and only for one unit: OutdoorGearLab's 1,710 Wh for the Explorer 2000 v2. It names an OutdoorGearLab AC180 test but gives no figure. No rival has measured figures for the S2000, C2000 Gen 2, Elite 200 V2, DELTA 2 Max or DELTA 3 Max, and no rival puts measurements side by side. unpluggedwatts.com (cited) could not be read: the fetch failed with an SSL certificate error and a curl retry was not approved. Its contents were not checked.
decides: This backs the low-price pick. The Anker SOLIX S2000 kit costs the least, and in tests it delivered the most energy at fridge-type loads: Notebookcheck about 1,900 Wh (95%), techtest.org 1,778–1,969 Wh. The C2000 Gen 2 does worse at the loads that matter in an outage, about 1,600 Wh (79%) at ~200 W in Notebookcheck's test of the EU unit. It only reaches about 1,850 Wh at 1,800 W. The Elite 200 V2 (1.91 kWh), DELTA 2 Max (1,800 Wh) and Explorer 2000 v2 (1,710–1,920 Wh, depending on the lab) all land within about 200 Wh of each other. Usable energy does not separate those three, so the choice between them stays on panel wattage in the kit and price. These tests come from different labs at different loads, so the figures are not one controlled comparison. A gap under about 10% should not decide a pick on its own.

findings.label: Usable AC energy (Notebookcheck)
findings.value: about 1,900 Wh of 2,000 Wh rated (about 95%) at a ~250 W AC load
findings.source_title: So leicht waren 2 Kilowattstunden noch nie: Anker Solix S2000 Powerstation im Praxis-Test
findings.note: Marcus Schwarten, Notebookcheck, 2026-10-07, German article. Which region's unit was tested is not stated. The same test drew about 2,400 Wh from the wall when charging at up to 1,100 W, so about 82% reached the battery and the round trip was about 78%. Bypass draw was about 3 W. Charging noise was about 35 dB. Idle with AC on lost about 10% of the battery per 24 h.

findings.label: Usable AC energy range (techtest.org)
findings.value: 1,778–1,969 Wh depending on load, average 1,893 Wh (about 95% of 2,000 Wh)
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX S2000 Test: Kompakte 2000-Wh-Powerstation mit extrem effizientem USV-Modus
findings.note: Michael Barton, techtest.org, 2026-10-04, EU 230 V unit. Three AC charges at 1,100 W used 2,440, 2,471 and 2,435 Wh (average 2,449 Wh). Round trip was 1,893 ÷ 2,449 = 77.3%. Idle with outlets on was 2.5–2.8 W. Load-by-load values appear only in a chart.

findings.label: Usable AC energy at low and high load (Notebookcheck)
findings.value: about 1,600 Wh of 2,048 Wh (just under 79%) at ~200 W; about 1,850 Wh (about 90%) at 1,800 W
findings.source_title: 11.6 kg lighter than its predecessor: Powerstation Anker Solix C2000 Gen 2 review
findings.note: Marcus Schwarten, Notebookcheck, first published 2026-02-24 and modified 2026-10-05. This was the EU unit, which the article says differs slightly from the US model. Notebookcheck itself calls the ~79% low-load result 'not a good value'. AC charging at up to 2,300 W drew almost 2,350 Wh from the wall (87% into the battery). Noise was about 35 dB at 1 m under high load.

findings.label: Usable energy discharged and energy to recharge (StorageReview)
findings.value: 1.91 kWh discharged of 2,073.6 Wh rated (about 92%); 2.44 kWh to recharge
findings.source_title: Portable Power Meets Lab-Grade Reliability: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Review
findings.note: Dylan Dougherty, StorageReview, 2025-04-25. The discharge load is not stated. Our arithmetic: 1,910 ÷ 2,073.6 = 92% of rated, and the round trip is 1.91 ÷ 2.44 = about 78%.

findings.label: Measured solar input (CleanTechnica)
findings.value: 520–600 W in sun, falling to about 245 W (125–600 W) under cloud; 25% to 100% from 12:00 to 3:39 pm
findings.note: CleanTechnica (author 'Z. S.'), 2025-07-07. Used 'two Bluetti solar panel arrays' with no model or wattage named, so this is not the 200 W or 2×200 W kit. It shows the unit took more than 400 W of solar when the panels supplied it. Wall charging took 0–100% in about 1 h 52 min.

findings.label: Usable AC energy and energy to recharge (StorageReview)
findings.value: 1,800 Wh through the AC inverter at a 350 W load (about 88% of 2,048 Wh); 2,370 Wh to recharge
findings.source_title: EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max Portable Power Station Review
findings.note: Kevin OBrien, StorageReview, 2023-07-09. Our arithmetic: 1,800 ÷ 2,048 = 87.9% of rated, and the round trip is 1,800 ÷ 2,370 = 76%.

findings.label: Usable AC energy (OutdoorGearLab)
findings.note: Chris McNamara with Kenji Mowrey, OutdoorGearLab, 2025-11-03. The page's table and text disagree. AC charging measured 817 Wh/h, 0–100% in 2.5 h. Measured weight was 38.9 lb. No solar wattage was measured. The rival powersized.com/best/solar-generator already cites the 1,710 Wh figure.

findings.label: Usable energy and wall energy (nextpit)
findings.value: 1,920 Wh delivered from 2,141 Wh drawn from the wall (89.6%)
findings.source_title: Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 im Test: Camping-Powerstation mit 2.000 Watt
findings.note: Thomas Kern, nextpit, 2025-02-21, German EU unit. The load is not stated. This is 210 Wh more than OutdoorGearLab measured, so the labs disagree by about 10%.

findings.label: Efficiency and idle draw (The Solar Lab)
findings.value: 79% efficiency; idle draw about 27 W; AC 0–100% in 68 min
findings.source_title: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Review: A Step Forward or a Step Sideways?
findings.note: The Solar Lab names no author and gives no date (footer says © 2026). It does not state the load behind the 79%. Our arithmetic: 79% × 2,048 Wh ≈ 1,618 Wh. That is our derivation, not a measured Wh figure. A 27 W idle draw is about 650 Wh a day, but this comes from an undated, unsigned single review.

unsourced: Measured solar input in watts or a measured refill time using each kit's own included panels (Elite 200 V2 + 200 W or 2×200 W, Explorer 2000 v2 + 2×SolarSaga 200 W, DELTA 2 Max or DELTA 3 Max + 2×220 W, S2000 + 200 W). I checked the OutdoorGearLab, Notebookcheck, StorageReview, nextpit, techtest.org and The Solar Lab reviews. None measured solar from the kit panels.

A measured usable-Wh figure, with a named author and date, for the base EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max. The Solar Lab gives only 79% efficiency. The Technology Man and AndroidGuys results tested the DELTA 3 Max Plus, a different model, and I did not open them.
Idle draw in watts for the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2. Notebookcheck only says it is 'significantly more economical when idle'.
A second lab's usable-Wh figure for the EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max. nextpit.com's review URL redirects to inside-digital.de, so I could not read it.

A Notebookcheck-style measured usable-Wh figure for the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2. Notebookcheck's Elite 200 V2 article is a news item based on BLUETTI's figures, not a test. I did not use the 2,065 Wh claim on backuppowerhub.com: I did not open the page, and 99.6% of rated through an inverter is not plausible.
Rival unpluggedwatts.com/2000-watt-power-station-comparison (cited by ChatGPT): I could not read it (SSL certificate error), so I did not check whether it has measurements.
